Hong Kong Technology Hardware Industry Hit by Ongoing Worker Walkout

A major walkout by workers in Hong Kong’s technology hardware industry has disrupted production lines and raised concerns among investors, with BYD Electronic International Co Ltd among the companies experiencing significant operational delays. The strike, which began early Monday morning, involves several hundred workers from factories across the New Territories and Kowloon, according to representatives from the Hong Kong Electronics Workers’ Union.

Workers are demanding higher wages and improved safety measures following a recent spate of workplace incidents. “The current base pay has not kept up with the rising cost of living in Hong Kong,” said union spokesperson Elaine Luk. “Our members want fair compensation and assurances that their well-being is a priority.”

Production at multiple facilities was reportedly halted, with several plants operating at reduced capacity as management scrambled to negotiate with union leaders. BYD Electronic International Co Ltd confirmed that some of its smartphone component lines were affected, estimating a daily output loss of 18%. “We are in active talks with employees and their representatives to resolve the situation as quickly as possible,” a company spokesperson said.

Analysts say the timing of the strike could have a pronounced impact on supply chains, especially with several hardware manufacturers already facing tight delivery schedules ahead of the third quarter. “Any prolonged disruption will likely lead to shipment delays and may force companies to revise their short-term forecasts,” said Peter Wong, an industry analyst at Hong Kong Capital Partners.

The Hong Kong Technology Hardware Association urged all parties to reach a swift resolution, citing the industry’s importance to the local economy. “This is a critical sector, and ongoing disruptions could have far-reaching consequences,” said association chairperson Rebecca Chan.

As negotiations continue, production remains partially suspended at several plants, with no clear indication of when a full resumption of operations might occur.
